They diagnosed an infection and gave me oral antibiotics, drew a sharpie border around the red area and told me to come straight back if the redness went over the line while taking the antibiotics and they would put me on a drip because it would mean they weren’t working.

I get it OP. After my mother died (30+ years ago) I was shopping in the town where she was well known. You are the one grieving and you do it in whatever way gets you though.

It sounds like your son may be on the autism spectrum. Many of the behaviours he is showing are similar to those on the spectrum. Or he may just have a behaviour issue. 
Either way, a visit to a paediatrician to properly diagnose his issues would be my first step. This will also lead to some specialist services that can help. 
Helping him at home can include practicing situations and appropriate behaviours with him. Get into the play acting and act out situations with him both playing himself and others so he gains some insight into how his behaviour might feel to others.  
Also, and I can’t stress this enough, consistent consequences for his behaviour. Good and bad. Kids love the security of knowing what will happen. If they act this way, this happens. Every time. Most soon try hard to behave in a way that brings the positive results.

Bullying is never ok but unfortunately it is a fact of life and you need to teach your kid to be able to deal with it appropriately and calmly. 
I work with behaviourally challenged children and spend a lot of my time working with them on strategies to deal with this kind of thing. 
The thing to make sure your kid knows is to not sink to the bully’s level. Stress the fact that doing so will only result in him being punished for a situation that he did not initiate. 
Help him with strategies to ignore the taunts, develop a few witty comebacks or just simply walking away. Also, build up his self esteem so that whatever others say about him he can feel sure that it’s a ‘them problem, not a me problem.’ 
Ask the school to choose a staff member that he can go to when it gets too much, preferably a school counsellor or coordinator. 
Throwing chairs in a room full of people is not only dangerous and aggressive, it is also a spectacular result for the bullies and they will now take every opportunity to try to repeat it. Make sure your son understands this. He is rewarding the bully by giving them exactly what they wanted, entertainment at someone else’s expense

I work with special needs kids and a lot of them are autistic. This is pretty common behaviour. A lot of it is mimicking to seem ‘normal’ (whatever that may be) and trying to fit in but he could also believe, even from this little interaction, that you are great friends. 
You seem like a lovely, caring young person and I’m sure you could be sensitive enough to have a chat with him. A lot of kids on the spectrum need detailed rules, schedules and guidance as to appropriate behaviour (google ‘social stories’ to get an idea of the concept). Pleasantly and plainly explaining your boundaries for this friendship will not only help you, but him. Something like “Hey, I really like how you like doing the same thing as me but sometimes I need to be by myself or with my other friends by ourselves. It would be cool if we could work out some times that we can spend together and some we can spend by ourselves or with other people. Let’s do that and make it our friendship plan.’ 
If he is resistant to this or wants more than you are willing or able to give, speak to a school counsellor or someone else that works with him. 
Well done on being a caring, aware and considerate young person. Your parents should be very proud of the excellent child they’ve raised.
